quercus-robur.edible: Acorns are edible only after repeated leaching to remove bitter tannins; historically ground into flour in lean years.
quercus-robur.medicinal: Bark rich in tannins was used traditionally as an astringent for sore throats and skin complaints.
quercus-robur.ecologicalRole: A keystone tree supporting over 2,000 species of insects, fungi, birds, and mammals; veteran oaks hold rare deadwood beetles.
quercus-robur.culturalUses: Timber for ships, barrels, and timber-framed buildings; a national emblem in England and a symbol of endurance.
quercus-robur.description: A broad, long-lived deciduous tree with deeply lobed leaves on very short stalks and acorns carried on long stems. Trunks become massive and fissured with age.

platanus-hispanica.ecologicalRole: Tolerates compacted soil and pollution, shading streets and cooling city air; its bark sheds in plates that discard grime.
platanus-hispanica.culturalUses: Planted along London's streets and squares since the 1700s, it is the capital's signature tree.
platanus-hispanica.description: A tall hybrid street tree with large maple-like leaves, spiky round fruit balls that hang through winter, and camouflage-patterned bark that flakes in patches.

betula-pendula.edible: Spring sap can be tapped as a lightly sweet drink; young leaves are added to teas.
betula-pendula.medicinal: Leaf tea was used traditionally as a mild diuretic and bark oil for skin conditions.
betula-pendula.ecologicalRole: A fast pioneer of open ground that enriches poor soils, feeds many moth caterpillars, and hosts fly agaric and other fungi.
betula-pendula.culturalUses: Bark used for tinder and canoes; twigs for besom brooms; a symbol of renewal in northern folklore.
betula-pendula.description: A graceful tree with peeling white bark marked by black diamonds, drooping twigs, and small triangular leaves with double-toothed edges.

fagus-sylvatica.edible: Beech nuts, or mast, are edible in small quantities when roasted; young spring leaves are mild in salads.
fagus-sylvatica.ecologicalRole: Casts deep shade that shapes whole woodland communities; mast years feed jays, mice, and wild boar.
fagus-sylvatica.culturalUses: Smooth grey bark has been carved with initials for centuries; wood is prized for furniture and firewood.
fagus-sylvatica.description: A stately tree with smooth silver-grey bark, oval leaves with wavy edges and silky hairs when young, and prickly husks that split to release triangular nuts.

aesculus-hippocastanum.edible: Not edible. Conkers contain aesculin and are toxic to people and dogs; they are unrelated to sweet chestnuts.
aesculus-hippocastanum.medicinal: Standardised seed extracts are used in Europe for poor leg circulation, but the raw seeds are poisonous.
aesculus-hippocastanum.ecologicalRole: Large candle-like flower spikes feed bees in late spring; the leaf-mining moth now browns most leaves by August.
aesculus-hippocastanum.culturalUses: Conkers are the classic British playground game every autumn.
aesculus-hippocastanum.description: A big spreading tree with hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets, white flower spikes in May, and glossy brown seeds inside spiny green cases.

tilia-europaea.edible: Young leaves are pleasant in salads; dried flowers make the classic linden tea.
tilia-europaea.medicinal: Linden flower tea is a traditional remedy for colds, anxiety, and restless sleep.
tilia-europaea.ecologicalRole: Flowers hum with bees in July; aphids on the leaves feed ladybirds and drip honeydew onto pavements below.
tilia-europaea.culturalUses: The village lime was a meeting place across central Europe; the soft wood is favoured by carvers.
tilia-europaea.description: A tall tree with heart-shaped, toothed leaves, sprouting shoots around the trunk base, and fragrant pale yellow flowers hanging beneath a narrow leafy bract.

ilex-aquifolium.edible: Not edible. The red berries cause vomiting if eaten.
ilex-aquifolium.ecologicalRole: Evergreen shelter for wintering birds; berries feed thrushes and the leaves host the holly blue butterfly.
ilex-aquifolium.culturalUses: Cut for midwinter and Christmas decorations for centuries; wood used for chess pieces and inlay.
ilex-aquifolium.description: An evergreen tree or shrub with glossy, spiny, dark green leaves that become smoother higher up, small white flowers, and bright red berries on female plants.

hedera-helix.edible: Not edible. Leaves and berries are mildly toxic.
hedera-helix.medicinal: Standardised leaf extracts are used in cough syrups; raw leaves can irritate skin.
hedera-helix.ecologicalRole: Autumn flowers are a vital late nectar source for bees and hoverflies; berries feed birds in winter and dense growth shelters bats and nesting wrens.
hedera-helix.culturalUses: A symbol of fidelity woven into wedding garlands; evergreen decoration in midwinter festivals.
hedera-helix.description: A woody evergreen climber with lobed juvenile leaves and unlobed adult leaves on flowering shoots; globular clusters of green-yellow flowers in autumn and black berries in spring.

crataegus-monogyna.edible: Young leaves were nibbled as 'bread and cheese'; haws are made into jelly and ketchup.
crataegus-monogyna.medicinal: Flowers, leaves, and berries are a long-standing traditional heart tonic; only under supervision.
crataegus-monogyna.ecologicalRole: Blossom feeds spring pollinators, thorny growth shelters nesting birds, and haws fuel migrating thrushes and waxwings.
crataegus-monogyna.culturalUses: The May tree of English folklore; the classic hedgerow plant of enclosed farmland.
crataegus-monogyna.description: A thorny small tree with deeply lobed leaves, frothy white or pink blossom in May, and clusters of dark red berries each holding a single stone.

sambucus-nigra.edible: Flowers flavour cordials and fritters; berries must be cooked before eating and are made into wine and jam.
sambucus-nigra.medicinal: Elderflower and elderberry preparations are traditional remedies for colds and flu; raw berries, leaves, and bark are mildly toxic.
sambucus-nigra.ecologicalRole: Fast-growing on disturbed ground; berries feed many birds and the flowers attract hoverflies.
sambucus-nigra.culturalUses: Surrounded by folklore about protection and witchcraft; hollow stems were made into whistles and pea-shooters.
sambucus-nigra.description: A shrub with pinnate leaves of five to seven leaflets, flat creamy flower heads in June, and drooping clusters of tiny black berries in late summer.

rubus-fruticosus.edible: Blackberries are sweet and safe when ripe; young shoots and leaves make tea.
rubus-fruticosus.medicinal: Leaf tea was a traditional treatment for diarrhoea and mouth ulcers thanks to its tannins.
rubus-fruticosus.ecologicalRole: Flowers feed bees for months and thickets shelter nesting birds, dormice, and hedgehogs; invasive where it smothers native scrub abroad.
rubus-fruticosus.description: An arching, prickly shrub with leaves of three to five toothed leaflets, white or pink flowers all summer, and fruits ripening from green through red to black.

urtica-dioica.edible: Young tops lose their sting when cooked and make a rich soup or a spinach substitute.
urtica-dioica.medicinal: Nettle tea and extracts are traditional for hay fever, joint pain, and as a spring tonic.
urtica-dioica.ecologicalRole: Larval food plant for peacock, small tortoiseshell, red admiral, and comma butterflies; a sign of nitrogen-rich soil.
urtica-dioica.culturalUses: Fibres were spun into cloth and rope; a folk remedy involved deliberate stinging for rheumatism.
urtica-dioica.description: An upright perennial with opposite, heart-shaped, sharply toothed leaves covered in stinging hairs and dangling strings of tiny green flowers.

taraxacum-officinale.edible: Young leaves are bitter salad greens, roots are roasted as a coffee substitute, and flowers are made into wine.
taraxacum-officinale.medicinal: Leaves are a traditional diuretic and the root a digestive bitter.
taraxacum-officinale.ecologicalRole: One of the most important early spring nectar and pollen sources for bees and hoverflies.
taraxacum-officinale.description: A rosette of toothed leaves with hollow stems that bleed milky sap, bright yellow flower heads, and the famous globe of parachuted seeds.

bellis-perennis.edible: Young leaves and flower buds can be added to salads in small amounts.
bellis-perennis.medicinal: Once known as bruisewort, it was applied to bruises and wounds in folk medicine.
bellis-perennis.ecologicalRole: Flowers nearly all year in short turf and feed small bees and hoverflies when little else is out.
bellis-perennis.culturalUses: Daisy chains and the 'loves me, loves me not' game are childhood classics.
bellis-perennis.description: A low perennial with spoon-shaped leaves in a flat rosette and single flower heads of white, pink-tipped petals around a yellow centre that close at night.

trifolium-pratense.edible: Flower heads are sweet and can be eaten raw or dried for tea.
trifolium-pratense.medicinal: Used traditionally for coughs and skin complaints; isoflavone extracts are sold for menopausal symptoms.
trifolium-pratense.ecologicalRole: Fixes nitrogen into the soil and is a top forage plant for bumblebees, especially long-tongued species.
trifolium-pratense.description: A meadow perennial with three oval leaflets, each often marked with a pale chevron, and round pink-purple flower heads.

plantago-major.edible: Very young leaves are edible cooked; older leaves are stringy. Seeds can be eaten like psyllium.
plantago-major.medicinal: Crushed leaves are a classic folk poultice for stings, cuts, and nettle rash.
plantago-major.ecologicalRole: Thrives in trampled ground and paths; seeds feed finches and sparrows.
plantago-major.culturalUses: Called 'white man's footprint' in North America because it followed European settlers' paths.
plantago-major.description: A ground-hugging rosette of broad oval leaves with strong parallel veins, sending up slender green flower spikes like rat tails.

achillea-millefolium.medicinal: Named for Achilles, who reputedly used it to staunch soldiers' wounds; still a traditional remedy for cuts, fever, and colds.
achillea-millefolium.ecologicalRole: Its flat flower heads are landing platforms for hoverflies, beetles, and solitary wasps; deep roots resist drought.
achillea-millefolium.culturalUses: Dried stalks were used for casting the I Ching in China.
achillea-millefolium.description: An aromatic perennial with soft, feathery, finely divided leaves and flat-topped clusters of tiny white or pink flowers.

digitalis-purpurea.edible: Not edible. Every part is highly poisonous and can stop the heart.
digitalis-purpurea.medicinal: The source of digoxin, a heart medicine; never self-administer, the margin between dose and poison is tiny.
digitalis-purpurea.ecologicalRole: Tubular flowers are tailored to bumblebees, which crawl inside following spotted guide marks.
digitalis-purpurea.culturalUses: Fairy folklore surrounds it; the spots inside the flowers were said to be fairy fingerprints.
digitalis-purpurea.description: A tall biennial with a rosette of soft, downy leaves in its first year and a spire of purple-pink, spotted tubular bells in its second.

allium-ursinum.edible: Leaves, flowers, and bulbs are edible with a mild garlic flavour; classic in pesto and soups. Beware of look-alikes like lily of the valley.
allium-ursinum.medicinal: Traditionally taken for blood pressure and as a spring cleanse, much like cultivated garlic.
allium-ursinum.ecologicalRole: Carpets ancient damp woodland in April and feeds early hoverflies; an indicator of old woodland.
allium-ursinum.culturalUses: Bear garlic in German and Slavic traditions, said to be eaten by bears waking from hibernation.
allium-ursinum.description: A woodland bulb with broad, glossy, elliptical leaves that smell strongly of garlic when crushed and starry white flowers in a rounded umbel.

hyacinthoides-non-scripta.edible: Not edible. All parts contain toxic glycosides.
hyacinthoides-non-scripta.ecologicalRole: About half the world's bluebells grow in Britain; carpets of them feed early bees and butterflies and indicate ancient woodland.
hyacinthoides-non-scripta.culturalUses: Protected by law in the UK; the sticky sap once glued feathers to arrows and bound books.
hyacinthoides-non-scripta.description: A spring bulb with narrow, strap-like leaves and one-sided, drooping spikes of fragrant violet-blue bells with curled-back petal tips and cream anthers.

ophrys-apifera.ecologicalRole: The flower mimics a female bee to lure males, though in Britain it mostly self-pollinates; a specialist of chalk and disturbed lime-rich ground.
ophrys-apifera.culturalUses: A prized find for botanists and a symbol of wild grassland restoration.
ophrys-apifera.description: A small orchid with a rosette of grey-green leaves and a few flowers with pink sepals and a velvety brown lip patterned like a bumblebee.

orchis-mascula.medicinal: Tubers were once made into salep, a thick drink sold before coffee arrived in Europe.
orchis-mascula.ecologicalRole: One of the first orchids to flower, offering no nectar but deceiving newly emerged bumblebees.
orchis-mascula.culturalUses: Shakespeare's 'long purples' in Hamlet; surrounded by love-potion folklore.
orchis-mascula.description: A woodland and grassland orchid with glossy leaves usually blotched with purple and a dense spike of purple flowers that smell faintly of tomcat.

dactylorhiza-fuchsii.ecologicalRole: The most frequent British orchid, colonising verges and old meadows; visited by bees and day-flying moths.
dactylorhiza-fuchsii.description: An orchid with narrow leaves spotted with dark purple and a conical spike of pale pink to lilac flowers, each lip marked with loops and dots and divided into three lobes.

fritillaria-meleagris.edible: Not edible. The bulbs and leaves are poisonous.
fritillaria-meleagris.ecologicalRole: A specialist of traditionally managed flood meadows, now rare; flowers are pollinated by early bumblebees.
fritillaria-meleagris.culturalUses: The county flower of Oxfordshire; famous displays draw visitors to Magdalen Meadow and Cricklade every April.
fritillaria-meleagris.description: A slender spring bulb with grassy leaves and nodding, lantern-shaped flowers chequered in purple and white, occasionally pure white.

primula-vulgaris.edible: Flowers are edible and used to decorate cakes and salads; leaves can be cooked.
primula-vulgaris.medicinal: Root and flower were traditional remedies for coughs and headaches.
primula-vulgaris.ecologicalRole: Among the first flowers of the year, feeding early bees, bee-flies, and brimstone butterflies.
primula-vulgaris.culturalUses: Primrose Day on 19 April commemorates Disraeli; a beloved emblem of spring in poetry.
primula-vulgaris.description: A low perennial with a rosette of crinkled, tongue-shaped leaves and pale yellow, five-petalled flowers with a deeper yellow eye, each on its own hairy stalk.

galanthus-nivalis.edible: Not edible. The bulbs are toxic and easily mistaken for onions.
galanthus-nivalis.medicinal: The source of galantamine, a drug used for early Alzheimer's disease; never use the raw plant.
galanthus-nivalis.ecologicalRole: Flowers in late winter when little else does, and opens on mild days to reward foraging bees.
galanthus-nivalis.culturalUses: A symbol of hope and Candlemas; 'galanthophiles' collect hundreds of named varieties.
galanthus-nivalis.description: A small bulb with two grey-green strap leaves and a single nodding white flower with three outer petals and a green-marked inner cup.

reynoutria-japonica.edible: Young spring shoots taste like sharp rhubarb and are cooked in Japan; harvesting it can spread fragments, so take care.
reynoutria-japonica.medicinal: The root is used in traditional East Asian medicine and is a commercial source of resveratrol.
reynoutria-japonica.ecologicalRole: Forms dense stands that shade out native plants along rivers and railways; its late flowers do feed bees.
reynoutria-japonica.description: A vigorous perennial with hollow, red-speckled bamboo-like stems, shield-shaped leaves with a flat base, and sprays of creamy flowers in late summer. Regrows from tiny root fragments.

impatiens-glandulifera.edible: Seeds are edible and nutty; young leaves can be cooked. Picking seeds before they pop is one way to help control it.
impatiens-glandulifera.ecologicalRole: Outcompetes riverbank plants and leaves banks bare to erosion in winter; its nectar-rich flowers distract bees from native species.
impatiens-glandulifera.culturalUses: Introduced to Victorian gardens in 1839 and nicknamed 'policeman's helmet' for its flower shape.
impatiens-glandulifera.description: A tall, fleshy annual with reddish hollow stems, lance-shaped toothed leaves in whorls, hooded pink flowers, and seed pods that explode at a touch.

heracleum-mantegazzianum.edible: Not edible. Do not touch: the sap causes severe burns and blistering in sunlight.
heracleum-mantegazzianum.ecologicalRole: Huge umbels feed insects, but colonies crowd out riverside plants and expose soil to erosion.
heracleum-mantegazzianum.description: A colossal umbellifer up to five metres tall with purple-blotched, bristly stems, deeply cut leaves over a metre wide, and umbrella-like white flower heads. A dangerous plant to handle.

rhododendron-ponticum.edible: Not edible. Leaves and nectar contain grayanotoxins; honey from it can cause 'mad honey' poisoning.
rhododendron-ponticum.ecologicalRole: Dense evergreen thickets acidify soil and shade out woodland flora; it also hosts the plant disease Phytophthora ramorum.
rhododendron-ponticum.culturalUses: Planted on Victorian estates for game cover and spring colour before its invasive nature was understood.
rhododendron-ponticum.description: A large evergreen shrub with leathery dark leaves and showy trusses of purple-pink funnel-shaped flowers in late spring.

buddleja-davidii.ecologicalRole: Flowers attract clouds of butterflies and moths, but seedlings colonise railways, walls, and brownfield land and can dominate native scrub.
buddleja-davidii.culturalUses: A cottage-garden staple since its introduction from China in the 1890s.
buddleja-davidii.description: A fast-growing shrub with arching branches, grey-green lance-shaped leaves, and long, honey-scented cones of lilac to purple flowers in summer.

prunus-laurocerasus.edible: Not edible. Leaves and seeds release cyanide; crushed leaves smell of almonds for that reason.
prunus-laurocerasus.ecologicalRole: Escapes from hedges into woodland where its heavy shade suppresses ground flora and tree regeneration.
prunus-laurocerasus.culturalUses: A common privacy hedge; the leaves were once used in killing jars by butterfly collectors.
prunus-laurocerasus.description: A dense evergreen shrub with large, glossy, leathery leaves, upright spikes of small white flowers in spring, and cherry-like fruits that ripen black.

lythrum-salicaria.medicinal: Traditionally used for diarrhoea and as a wound wash thanks to its tannins.
lythrum-salicaria.ecologicalRole: A rich nectar plant of British wetlands, but a serious invader of North American marshes where it displaces native plants.
lythrum-salicaria.description: A wetland perennial with square stems, opposite lance-shaped leaves, and tall dense spikes of magenta six-petalled flowers in summer.

jacobaea-vulgaris.edible: Not edible. Contains liver-damaging alkaloids; toxic to horses and cattle, especially when dried in hay.
jacobaea-vulgaris.ecologicalRole: Supports around 30 specialist insects, including the black-and-yellow cinnabar moth caterpillar, and is a rich nectar source.
jacobaea-vulgaris.culturalUses: Nicknamed 'stinking Willie' in Scotland after the Duke of Cumberland; the subject of long-running weed control debates.
jacobaea-vulgaris.description: A biennial with a rosette of deeply lobed, dark green leaves and flat clusters of golden yellow daisy-like flowers on stems up to a metre tall.

chamaenerion-angustifolium.edible: Young shoots can be cooked like asparagus; fermented leaves make the Russian tea 'Ivan chai'.
chamaenerion-angustifolium.medicinal: Leaf tea was a folk remedy for digestive and prostate complaints.
chamaenerion-angustifolium.ecologicalRole: A pioneer of burnt and cleared ground, hence 'fireweed'; flowers feed bees and the leaves host the elephant hawk-moth.
chamaenerion-angustifolium.culturalUses: Nicknamed 'bombweed' after it covered London's bomb sites in the 1940s.
chamaenerion-angustifolium.description: A tall perennial with narrow, willow-like leaves spiralling up the stem and long spires of rose-pink four-petalled flowers followed by fluffy seeds.

symphytum-officinale.edible: Not for eating. Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that damage the liver.
symphytum-officinale.medicinal: Known as knitbone: leaf poultices are used externally for sprains and bruises, never internally.
symphytum-officinale.ecologicalRole: Deep-rooted and rich in nutrients; flowers are worked by bumblebees, some of which bite holes to rob the nectar.
symphytum-officinale.culturalUses: Gardeners steep leaves for a potent liquid fertiliser.
symphytum-officinale.description: A robust, bristly perennial with large, rough, lance-shaped leaves running down the stem and curled clusters of purple, pink, or cream bell flowers.

filipendula-ulmaria.edible: Sweet-scented flowers flavour cordials, mead, and desserts.
filipendula-ulmaria.medicinal: Contains salicylates and was the plant from which aspirin was named; a traditional remedy for fever, pain, and heartburn.
filipendula-ulmaria.ecologicalRole: A wetland and ditch plant whose frothy flowers attract hoverflies and beetles.
filipendula-ulmaria.culturalUses: A sacred herb of the Druids and a medieval strewing herb for floors.
filipendula-ulmaria.description: A tall damp-meadow perennial with pinnate leaves, white underneath, and dense frothy clusters of creamy white flowers that smell of almonds and honey.

mentha-aquatica.edible: Leaves are used like garden mint for teas, sauces, and drinks.
mentha-aquatica.medicinal: A traditional digestive and remedy for headaches, like other mints.
mentha-aquatica.ecologicalRole: A pondside plant whose flowers attract bees, hoverflies, and butterflies in late summer.
mentha-aquatica.description: An aromatic perennial of wet ground with hairy, toothed oval leaves, often purple-tinged, and rounded heads of lilac-pink flowers at the stem tips.

rosa-canina.edible: Rose hips are rich in vitamin C and are made into syrup, jelly, and tea; remove the irritant seed hairs first.
rosa-canina.medicinal: Rosehip syrup was given to children in wartime Britain against scurvy and is still used for joint health.
rosa-canina.ecologicalRole: Flowers feed bees and hoverflies; hips feed birds and small mammals through winter; thorny stems shelter nests.
rosa-canina.culturalUses: The wild rose of English heraldry and folklore.
rosa-canina.description: An arching, thorny shrub with pinnate leaves of five to seven leaflets, pale pink five-petalled flowers in June, and glossy red oval hips in autumn.

corylus-avellana.edible: Hazelnuts are edible raw or roasted and ripen in September, if squirrels leave any.
corylus-avellana.ecologicalRole: Coppiced hazel creates the dappled woodland that dormice, fritillary butterflies, and spring flowers depend on.
corylus-avellana.culturalUses: Rods for hurdles, thatching spars, and walking sticks; forked twigs for water divining.
corylus-avellana.description: A multi-stemmed shrub with rounded, soft, double-toothed leaves, yellow catkins in February, and nuts in leafy husks.
